groups.title: Relational Databases
groups.question: Explain how you would design and query tables for users and their orders in a relational database.

followUps.SQL — JOINs, Transactions & EXPLAIN: Why must a money transfer run inside a transaction, and what does EXPLAIN tell you about a slow query?
followUps.Schema Design — Normalization & Foreign: What goes wrong when the same fact is stored in two tables, and how do foreign keys protect you?

evidence.text: A transfer is several writes that must all succeed or all roll back, so money never disappears or doubles.
EXPLAIN shows the query plan: whether it uses an index or scans the whole table, and the estimated cost.
JOINs combine related tables on a condition; a missing condition returns every combination of rows.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (JOIN, transaction, EXPLAIN) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says EXPLAIN makes a slow query faster or fixes it.

evidence.text: Each fact is stored in one place, so it can't be updated in one table and left stale in another.
A foreign key makes the database reject rows that point at a parent that doesn't exist, so no orphans pile up.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (normalization, foreign key) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says foreign keys exist mainly to make queries faster.

groups.title: Connecting Databases to Node.js
groups.question: Explain how your Node.js API should connect to and query a SQL database safely and efficiently.

followUps.Connection Pooling with node-postgres (p: Why reuse a pool of connections instead of opening one per request?
followUps.Parameterized Queries & SQL Injection Pr: Why does a parameterized query stop SQL injection when building the SQL string yourself doesn't?

evidence.text: Opening a database connection is slow (network handshake and authentication), so doing it on every request adds latency and load.
A pool keeps a set of open connections that requests borrow and give back.
The pool size is a limit: too small and requests queue, too large and the database is overloaded.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (connection pool, pg) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says one pooled connection can run unlimited queries in parallel.

evidence.text: A parameterized query sends the SQL text and the values separately.
The database treats the values only as data, so input can never change the structure of the query.
Building the string yourself lets input like a quote end the string and add its own SQL.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (parameterized query, SQL injection) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says removing quotes from user input is a full fix.

groups.title: NoSQL with MongoDB
groups.question: Explain how you would model and query blog posts and their comments in MongoDB.

followUps.Document Model — Embedding vs Referencin: When would you embed comments inside the post, and when store them separately?
followUps.Indexes & the Aggregation Pipeline: Why should $match come early in an aggregation pipeline?

evidence.text: Embed when the data is always read with the parent and stays bounded in size.
Reference it when it grows without limit, is shared, or is queried and updated on its own.
Embedding gives one read but big or duplicated documents; referencing needs extra queries or $lookup.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (embed, reference, document) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says MongoDB can't relate documents at all, so data must always be embedded.

evidence.text: An aggregation pipeline passes documents through its stages in order.
A $match at the start can use an index and cuts the number of documents straight away.
Placed after reshaping stages, $match can't use the index, so every document flows through the earlier stages.

notEnough: Only naming the terms ($match, aggregation pipeline) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says stage order never matters because MongoDB reorders everything.

groups.title: Indexing Strategies
groups.question: Explain how indexes make queries fast, and how you choose which ones to create.

followUps.B-tree Indexes & Composite Index Column: Why is an index on (status, created_at) different from one on (created_at, status)?
followUps.Partial & Covering Indexes: What is a covering index, and why can it answer a query without reading the table?

evidence.text: A composite index is sorted by its first column, then by the next column within that.
It helps queries that filter on the leading column; a query on only the second column can't use it well.
So columns are ordered to match how you query, usually equality filters first.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (composite index, B-tree) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says column order in a composite index makes no difference.

evidence.text: A covering index contains every column the query needs.
So the database answers from the index alone without reading the table rows.
A partial index only includes rows that match a condition, which keeps it small and fast.

notEnough: Only naming the terms (covering index, partial index) without explaining how they work or why they matter.

misconceptions.text: Says a covering index means indexing every column of the table.
